price_per_million.source: openrouter.ai/models, confirmed via preflight 2026-11-11; thinking tokens billed as output

research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent H2-H1 change
team-level trait reliability (split-half and year-to-year persistence)
regression to the mean in H2-H1 differences
methodological_questions: Is a defense's opponent-adjusted H2-H1 effect reproducible across split halves of a season and across seasons?
Is the signal-to-noise ratio of per-team H2-H1 differences adequate with about 82 games (plus playoffs) per team-season?
How are regression to the mean, the mechanical H1-H2 coupling, opponent strength and score state handled?
What reliability statistic and null or placebo comparison suit 120 team-seasons?

historical_evidence.finding: H1 reliance on a play type did not predict H2 suppression beyond mean reversion. BH-adjusted tests were null or WEAK. Top-1 accuracy was 0.550 against a mean-reversion baseline of 0.511 (+0.039). The record says the bulk of H2 suppression is regression to the mean. Sample: 8873 team-games.

Connector quality Q_p had split-half r=+0.215 (Spearman-Brown about 0.355) and ICC 0.216, with 78.4% of variance within-player. The record judged it too unreliable to treat as a stable scoutable trait (n=102).

The A1 adaptation PPP lift failed falsification: wrong-way teams were not worse than no-signal teams, and there was no carryover to the next game. The failure mechanism is recorded as a construction, selection or labelling artifact, with label error and regression-to-the-mean limitations.

Player-level residual structural influence showed split-half stability (pooled rho about +0.67 to +0.69). This is a different construct, but split-half reliability testing was feasible and informative there.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using H1 behaviour to predict H2 suppression.
failed_approaches.why: Predictive lift over the mean-reversion baseline was tiny; the effect was mostly regression to the mean (B_powered_null).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating a noisy on-off-style player-season quantity as a stable trait.
failed_approaches.why: Low split-half reliability (low_measurement_reliability); most variance was within-unit noise.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Interpreting a PPP change after an inferred adaptation as a real response.
failed_approaches.why: Selection, regression-to-the-mean and label-error artifacts; no carryover.

evidence_establishes: Earlier work in this project found that apparent H2 changes and suppression are largely explained by regression to the mean (FAM:SF-APPS-070, status rejected).
Half-split and noise-dominated difference measures have previously shown low reliability (FAM:SF-APPS-085, untestable) or artifactual effects (FAM:SF-APPA-001).
Split-half reliability is an established method here and can return strong stability for some constructs (FAM:SF18).
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record measures the team-level, opponent-adjusted H2-H1 effect of a defense or its reliability across seasons.
The retrieved records involve different constructs (play-type usage, connector quality, adapter labels, player influence), so they give no direct estimate of this trait's reliability.
None tests persistence across the four seasons of 2022-23 to 2025-26.
own_inferences: The H2-H1 change is a difference of two noisy halves with strong mechanical coupling to H1 level, so the per-team signal-to-noise ratio is probably low and reliability probably well below 0.3.
Most of any apparent team effect will probably come from the opponents' own H2-H1 tendencies, score state, garbage time and rest or rotation patterns, not from defensive identity.
The team-season count is adequate to detect moderate persistence (r of about 0.3 or more) but not small persistence.
The likeliest result is a null or a low-reliability finding; a positive result would need strong artifact checks.
uncertainties: The true between-team SD of the trait relative to game-level noise (H2-H1 point margins have large SD) is unknown.
It is unclear how many of the 120 team-seasons are independent (about 30 teams x 4 seasons; the 2025-26 playoffs are partly small-n).
Which H2-H1 metric (PPP, points, eFG%) is best is unsettled, as is whether garbage-time filtering biases it.
The retrieval returned only four loosely related records.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the history I might have proceeded as a plain trait-reliability test. The records (regression to the mean in FAM:SF-APPS-070, low split-half reliability in FAM:SF-APPS-085, adaptation artifacts in FAM:SF-APPA-001) led me to require opponent adjustment, a mean-reversion null, a reliability-based stopping rule, and lower expected support.

blocking_constraints.text: If the split-half reliability of the H2-H1 effect is near zero, the persistence question cannot be answered beyond 'not a reliable trait'.
There are only 120 team-seasons (about 90 season-to-season pairs), which detects only r of about 0.3 or more at 80% power.

prior_work.summary: Nothing directly answers the team-trait question. Related work indicates H2 changes are dominated by regression to the mean, and that noisy difference-type constructs often have low split-half reliability or are artifacts.

risks.text: The H2-H1 difference has high noise relative to its signal, and split-half reliability may be very low.
H2 outcomes regress toward the mean given H1, and teams selected for extreme H2-H1 effects will regress in later samples.
H2-H1 is mechanically negatively related to H1 level, so opponent H1 strength must be controlled or the metric modelled as an H2 outcome given H1.
Opponent offensive quality and its own H2 tendencies, home/away, rest, score state and garbage time, starters' minutes, injuries and the team's own offense all confound the defense's effect.
Only 120 team-seasons are available, and playoff samples are tiny.
Roster, coaching and rule changes between seasons make year-to-year persistence an under-estimate of within-season reliability.
Reliability must be compared with a permutation null (shuffled team labels within opponent) and not only with zero.
Multiple metrics, splits and season pairs would inflate false positives unless one primary metric is fixed in advance.

design.estimand: The between-team variance share of each defense's opponent-adjusted H2-H1 effect, defined as the team random effect in a model for opponent PPP in H2 given opponent H1 PPP and covariates. Reliability is the split-half ICC (odd/even games) and the year-to-year correlation of team effects.
design.unit: Team-season (defense), with game-level observations nested within it (opponent-game).
design.sample: Regular season 2022-23 through 2025-26 (120 team-seasons), complete-data version only. Exclude playoffs from the primary analysis and use them as a sensitivity check. Exclude overtime and garbage-time possessions (a pre-registered margin rule, such as a margin of 20 or more in the last 6 minutes of the 4th quarter).
design.power: About 90 consecutive-season pairs give 80% power for r of about 0.29 (alpha 0.05). For split-half reliability, a pre-registered threshold of Spearman-Brown reliability of at least 0.5 is 'reliable', and below 0.3 is 'not reliable'. Report CIs by bootstrap over games and teams. If the lower CI bound on split-half reliability is below 0.2, report 'not distinguishable from noise'.
design.controls: A mixed model with opponent H1 PPP (mean reversion), opponent season offense rating, the defense's own H1 PPP, home/away, rest days, score state at half and starters' minutes; random effects for team-defense and opponent. Handle regression to the mean by modelling H2 given H1 and not the raw difference.
design.falsification: A permutation null (shuffle defense labels across games within opponent, and re-run split-half); a placebo using the team's own offensive H2-H1 change; and a comparison with a pure mean-reversion baseline, as in FAM:SF-APPS-070. Also check whether the stability survives the garbage-time exclusion.
design.multiplicity: One primary metric (H2 PPP given H1 PPP), one primary reliability statistic (split-half ICC), and one year-to-year test. Secondary metrics (eFG%, turnovers) are exploratory with BH correction.
design.decision_rule: Supported only if the primary split-half reliability is at least 0.5 with the lower CI bound above the permutation-null 95th percentile, and the year-to-year r is positive with CI excluding 0. Rejected if the CI upper bound for reliability is below 0.3. Otherwise inconclusive.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files, 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons (the 2025-26 regular season complete from 2026-04-13), frozen at the analysis date with its hash recorded; derived play-type records are not required.

research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent second-half change
methodological_questions: Is a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change stable across seasons or split samples?
How large is the sample of games/possessions per team-season relative to noise in H2-H1 differences?
How should regression to the mean, opponent strength, and score-state/garbage-time confounding be handled?
What reliability metric and null/placebo comparison are appropriate with 120 team-seasons?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether more tool calls are worth it; the budget allows, but I think I have enough to finalize. I'm considering a quick re-read of one family for SF-APPS-070, though it isn't strictly necessary, since the cited statuses just need to be exact. Next I'm checking the design: 120 team-seasons (30 teams across four seasons), with the estimand being each team's defensive effect on opponents.

I'm working out the design now: 120 team-seasons, opponent-adjusted, with noise from roughly 82 games per team and reliability likely low. I'm checking statistical power for the year-to-year correlations and listing the risks I need to guard against, such as confounding, regression to the mean, and mechanical artifacts. My provisional call is to proceed with changes, since rejection or uncertainty seems most likely.

I'm noting that the 2025-26 playoffs finish on 2026-06-21, so I'll keep them separate and either exclude them or run a sensitivity check. Looking at the historical cases: SF-APPS-070 was rejected because most of the second-half suppression is regression to the mean, SF-APPS-085 was untestable given low split-half reliability, and SF18 was supported on split-half stability for a different construct, which shows the method can work. SF-APPA-001 was flagged as an artifact because of flaws in the adaptation construct.
